summary: Gives guidelines for defining binary packet timestamp formats in network protocols at various layers, and recommends three timestamp formats. It helps protocol designers avoid common pitfalls. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8877 is a design guide for the timestamps that network protocols put in their packets. It lists the questions every such design has to answer, such as how long the field is, what the units are and when the value wraps around, and then offers three formats that can simply be reused: two from the Network Time Protocol and one taken from the Precision Time Protocol.

subtitle: A template for designing binary timestamps, and three ready-made formats taken from NTP and PTP.

tldr.problem: Every network protocol that puts a timestamp in a packet has to decide on a binary format, and protocols that invent their own make it harder to reuse hardware timestamping and to combine with clock synchronisation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a template that a timestamp specification must fill in, covering size, units, resolution, wraparound, epoch and leap seconds, and recommends three concrete formats: the NTP 64-bit and 32-bit timestamps and the truncated PTP timestamp.
tldr.outcome: A new protocol is expected to reuse one of the three formats, and where none fits it should derive its own from an existing one and say why. The RFC also sets out what a protocol must say about synchronisation and about the security of the timestamps it carries.

today: RFC 8877 is an Informational document from September 2020 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It remains a design guide for protocol authors: new protocols that need a packet timestamp are expected to reuse one of its three recommended formats rather than define a new one.

sections.title: What Packet Timestamps Are For
sections.content:
Timestamps are widely used in network protocols for various purposes: for logging or reporting the time of an event, for messages in delay measurement and clock synchronization protocols, and as part of a value that is unlikely to repeat, a nonce, in security protocols.

In the RFC series timestamps appear in one of two forms. Text-based timestamps are represented as user-friendly strings and are widely used, for example in information objects and data models. Packet timestamps, on the other hand, are represented by a compact binary field that has a fixed size, are not intended to have a human-friendly format, and are also very common, used for example for measuring delay and for synchronizing clocks.

The document presents guidelines for defining a packet timestamp format in network protocols, and three recommended timestamp formats. It is expected that a new network protocol requiring a packet timestamp will, in most cases, use one of these recommended formats; a protocol may use more than one, and where none of the recommended formats fits, the new protocol specification should define its own format following the guidelines in the document.

The rationale for a small set of recommended formats is significant reuse. Network protocols can typically reuse the timestamp format of the Network Time Protocol or the Precision Time Protocol, which allows straightforward integration with an NTP- or PTP-based timer. Moreover, since accurate timestamping mechanisms are often implemented in hardware, a protocol that reuses an existing format can be deployed quickly using existing hardware timestamping capabilities.

The document also defines the terms it uses. A timestamp is a value representing a point in time, corresponding to an event that occurred or is scheduled to occur. The timestamp error is the difference between the timestamp value and the value of a reference clock at the time of the event the timestamp was meant to indicate. Timestamp accuracy is the mean of the timestamp error over an ensemble of measurements, timestamp precision is the variation of that error over an ensemble of measurements, and timestamp resolution is the minimal time unit used to represent the timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: Some protocols need to say when something happened, either for measuring delay, for keeping clocks in step, or simply to make a value that will not repeat. This RFC is about the binary version of that, the fixed-size field carried in a packet, and it argues that most protocols should stop inventing their own and reuse one of three standard ones.

sections.title: The Template for a Timestamp Specification
sections.content:
The document recommends using the timestamp formats it defines. Where those do not satisfy the protocol's requirements, the specification should clearly state the reasons for defining a new format, and it is recommended to derive the new format from an existing one, either one from this document or any previously defined format. The specification must unambiguously define the syntax and semantics of the timestamp, and in some cases additional attributes or aspects will need to be defined.

The template requires at least the following. Size: the number of bits or octets used to represent the packet timestamp field, and the size of each field if the timestamp is made up of more than one. Network order, meaning big endian, is assumed by default, and if that is not the case the specification says so explicitly. Units: the units used to represent the timestamp, and the units of each field if there is more than one, together with the permitted range of values where a field is limited. Resolution: the resolution is equal to the timestamp field unit, and if the timestamp consists of two or more fields using different time units, the resolution is the smallest time unit. Wraparound: the period after which the value repeats, together with any further wraparound-related considerations. Epoch: the origin of the timescale used for the timestamp, the moment in time used as a reference for the timestamp value. The epoch may be based on a standard time scale such as UTC, or it may be a relative timestamp whose epoch is the time at which the device was powered up, which is not affected by leap seconds. Leap seconds: whether the timestamp is affected by leap seconds, and if so, that it represents the time elapsed since the epoch minus the number of leap seconds that have occurred since the epoch.

The specification of a protocol that uses a packet timestamp is also expected to cover the synchronization aspects of using the timestamp. While those aspects are not strictly part of the timestamp format specification, they provide the necessary context for using the timestamp within the scope of the protocol. In some cases timestamps are used without any synchronization, for example a timestamp that indicates the number of seconds since power-up, and the Synchronization Aspects section then says that the timestamp does not correspond to a synchronized time reference and may discuss how that affects its use.
sections.plainLanguage: Every timestamp design has to answer the same handful of questions: how many bits, what unit, how fine the resolution, when does the number repeat, what moment counts as zero, and are leap seconds allowed to disturb it. The RFC lists them as a template that a specification must fill in, and adds one more: say how the clocks are kept in step, or say that they are not.

sections.title: The Three Recommended Formats
sections.content:
Different protocols have different requirements and constraints, so the choice of format may depend on several factors. The size of the timestamp field may be constrained in some protocols. The resolution may matter directly, and extensibility is a potentially important factor: it may be desirable to allow a format to be extended to a higher resolution, as the NTP 32-bit format can be improved to the NTP 64-bit format in a straightforward way. The wraparound period, the length of the interval in which the timestamp is unique, together with the resolution, determines the number of bits needed. And a common format should be preferred where two or more protocols that are often used together both carry timestamps: a protocol typically run on a PC may integrate more easily with an NTP-synchronized timer, while a protocol deployed on a hardware-based platform may make better use of a PTP-based timestamp.

The NTP 64-bit timestamp format is defined in RFC 5905 and is used in several network protocols, including RFC 6374, RFC 4656 and RFC 5357, and should be preferred in protocols typically deployed in concert with NTP. It has a 32-bit Seconds field giving the integer portion of the number of seconds since the epoch, and a 32-bit Fraction field whose unit is 2^(-32) seconds, roughly 233 picoseconds. The epoch is 1 January 1900 at 00:00 UTC. Strictly speaking, UTC did not exist before 1 January 1972, but it is convenient to assume it always has, so the timestamp specifies the number of seconds since 1 January 1972 at 00:00 UTC plus 2272060800, the number of seconds between the two dates. The format is affected by leap seconds, so the value represents the number of seconds elapsed since the epoch minus the number of leap seconds, and during and possibly before or after a leap second the value may be temporarily ambiguous. The resolution is 2^(-32) seconds, and the format wraps around every 2^32 seconds, roughly 136 years, with the next wraparound in 2036.

The NTP 32-bit timestamp format is also defined in RFC 5905 and is used in the METRICS and NSHMD specifications. It should be preferred in protocols typically deployed in concert with NTP, and can be used when space constraints do not allow the 64-bit format or when the 32-bit format meets the resolution and wraparound requirements. It has a 16-bit Seconds field and a 16-bit Fraction field whose unit is 2^(-16) seconds, roughly 15.3 microseconds. The epoch is again 1 January 1900 at 00:00 UTC, with the same note about 2272060800, and the format is affected by leap seconds in the same way. The resolution is 2^(-16) seconds, and it wraps around every 2^16 seconds, roughly 18 hours.

The PTP truncated timestamp format is a 64-bit field holding the 64 least significant bits of the 80-bit timestamp used by the Precision Time Protocol. It was defined in IEEE 1588 version 1 and is used in several protocols, such as RFC 6374, RFC 7456, RFC 8186 and ITU-T Y.1731, and should be preferred in protocols typically deployed in PTP-capable devices. It has a 32-bit Seconds field and a 32-bit Nanoseconds field whose value is in the range 0 to 10^9 minus 1. The PTP epoch is 1 January 1970 00:00:00 TAI. This format is not affected by leap seconds, its resolution is 1 nanosecond, and it wraps around every 2^32 seconds, roughly 136 years, with the next wraparound in 2106.
sections.plainLanguage: Three formats are offered. Two come from the Network Time Protocol: a wide one with 32 bits of seconds and 32 bits of fraction, and a narrow one with 16 bits of each that repeats about every eighteen hours. The third is a cut-down version of the Precision Time Protocol timestamp, which counts in nanoseconds and ignores leap seconds.

sections.title: Synchronization Aspects and Leap Seconds
sections.content:
A specification that defines a new timestamp format, or uses one of the recommended formats, should include a Synchronization Aspects section. The recommended formats themselves do not include the synchronization aspects, but the protocol specifications that use them are expected to. That section should specify all the assumptions and requirements related to synchronization, for example whether the nodes populating the timestamps should be synchronized among themselves, and whether the timestamp is measured with respect to a central reference clock such as an NTP server. If time is assumed to be synchronized to a time standard such as UTC or TAI, that should be specified there, as should the required timestamp accuracy and precision.

Leap second considerations belong in the same section. A leap second is a one-second adjustment occasionally applied to UTC to keep it aligned with solar time, and it may be positive or negative, with the clock shifted one second forward or backward. All leap seconds so far have been in the backward direction, and the document focuses on that common case. In a timekeeping system that considers leap seconds, the system clock may be affected in one of three ways: the clock is turned backwards one second at the end of the leap second; the clock is frozen during the duration of the leap second; or the clock is slowed down during the leap second and adjacent intervals until the new time value catches up, an interval commonly called leap smear, which can range from several seconds to several hours before, during or after the leap second.

How leap seconds are handled depends on the synchronization protocol, so the document does not specify it. However, if a timestamp format is defined with respect to a timescale affected by leap seconds, the Synchronization Aspects section should say how the use of leap seconds affects the use of the timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: Having agreed on the shape of the timestamp, a protocol still has to say where the time comes from. Are the machines running it keeping their clocks in step with each other, or with UTC, or with an atomic time standard, or not at all? The RFC also explains the awkward business of leap seconds, where the clock is either held back, frozen, or slowed, and asks protocols to say which behaviour their timestamps assume.

sections.title: Formats in Use and Two Example Specifications
sections.content:
Packet timestamps are used in many network protocols, with delay measurement, clock synchronization and other uses. The document lists a non-exhaustive set of the protocols that use them and the formats they use. NTP, the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol and TWAMP use the NTP 64-bit format, as does the later TWAMP specification, which also uses the PTP truncated format. TRILL and MPLS use the PTP truncated format. TCP, RTP, IPFIX and BinaryTime use other formats. The METRICS specification uses both NTP formats, and NSHMD uses the NTP 32-bit and the PTP truncated formats.

Two example specifications follow, showing the text needed when a protocol reuses a recommended format. In the first, the protocol uses the NTP 64-bit format, and the synchronization section says the nodes running it are assumed to be synchronized to UTC by a mechanism outside the scope of the document. In typical deployments the protocol runs on a machine that uses NTP for synchronization, so the timestamp may be derived from the NTP-synchronized clock and measured with respect to the clock of an NTP server. Because the NTP time format is affected by leap seconds, the timestamp is too, and its value during and possibly before or after a leap second may be temporarily inaccurate.

In the second, the protocol uses the PTP truncated format, and the synchronization section says the nodes are assumed to be synchronized among themselves, that they may be synchronized to a global reference time, and that if PTP is used for synchronization the timestamp may be derived from the PTP-synchronized clock and measured with respect to a PTP grandmaster clock.

Some protocols also carry a control field describing the structure, format, content and properties of the timestamps. Such control information can be conveyed by a dedicated control plane protocol or made available at the management plane, for example with a YANG data model, and an optional control field lets some of that information travel attached to the timestamp. The Error Estimate field of OWAMP is an example of a packet timestamp control field, as are the Root Dispersion and Root Delay fields in the NTP header, which give information about timestamp precision, and the Correction Field in the PTP header, whose value corrects for the delay along the path and may be updated by transit nodes. The document sets out high-level requirements for such a control field: an extensible feature set, a size trade-off between supported features and field size, composition, so that applications can rely on specific elements being present, with each element mandatory, conditionally mandatory or optional, and a category distinction between static information such as the timestamp size and semantics, which is typically valid throughout a session and may be conveyed once at session establishment, and runtime information such as the estimated accuracy at the time of sampling, which augments each timestamp instance and can be costly in a high-traffic protocol. Proposals for timestamp control fields are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Several well-known protocols already use these formats, and the RFC shows the two paragraphs a new protocol needs to write when it borrows one. It also covers the optional extra field some protocols carry alongside the timestamp, which describes how accurate the timestamp is, whether it needs leap-second handling, and what clock it is measured against.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A network protocol that uses a packet timestamp MUST specify the security considerations that result from using the timestamp. The document gives an overview of the common ones.

Any metadata attached to control or data packets, and specifically packet timestamps, can facilitate network reconnaissance. By passively eavesdropping on timestamped packets, an attacker can gather information about the network performance and the level of synchronization between nodes.

In some cases timestamps could be spoofed or modified by on-path attackers, attacking the application that uses them. In a delay measurement protocol, for example, an attacker can modify en route timestamps in a way that manipulates the measurement results. Integrity protection mechanisms such as Message Authentication Codes can mitigate such attacks; the specification of such a mechanism is outside the scope of this document, as integrity protection is typically defined per network protocol and not specifically for the timestamp field.

Delay attacks have a similar impact: an attacker maliciously delays some or all of the en route messages. Mitigating them is a significant challenge, and unlike spoofing and modification they cannot be prevented by cryptographic integrity protection. In some cases they can be mitigated by sending the timestamped information through multiple paths, which allows detection of and resistance to an attacker with access to one of the paths.

Finally, timestamping relies on an underlying synchronization mechanism, so any attack that compromises the synchronization mechanism also compromises the protocols that use timestamping. Attacks on time protocols are discussed in RFC 7384.
sections.plainLanguage: Timestamps leak information: an observer can learn how well the network is performing and how closely the machines are synchronised. They can also be altered in transit to bend a delay measurement, which a message authentication code can prevent. Delaying them cannot be prevented that way, and a compromise of the clock synchronisation itself undermines everything that depends on it.

viz.caption: WHAT A TIMESTAMP SPECIFICATION MUST ANSWER

items.title: Size
items.text: The number of bits or octets used for the field, and the size of each field if there is more than one. Big endian is assumed unless stated otherwise.

items.title: Units
items.text: The units used to represent the timestamp, and the permitted range of values where a field is limited.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: Equal to the field unit, or the smallest time unit if the timestamp has several fields.

items.title: Wraparound
items.text: The period after which the value repeats, and any further wraparound considerations.

items.title: Epoch
items.text: The origin of the timescale: a standard such as UTC, or a relative moment such as the time the device was powered up.

items.title: Leap seconds
items.text: Whether the timestamp is affected by leap seconds, and if so, that it counts elapsed seconds minus the leap seconds that have occurred.
